entry.title: India needs tax reform to reduce distortions and lift investment growth
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India needs tax reform to reduce distortions and lift investment growthIndia needs tax reform to reduce distortions and lift investment growth

Recent tax changes are welcome, but India needs sustained reforms to address exemptions, reduce cascading taxes, improve compliance and broaden the tax base without distorting investment decisions.

premium

India needs continuous tax reforms to broaden the tax base, reduce exemptions and minimise distortions in investment and economic activity, argues M Govinda Rao.| Illustration: Binay Sinha

M Govinda Rao6 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 9:53 PM ISTUnless threatened by a crisis, the natural tendency of governments is to prefer the status quo in economic policies, particularly in tax policy. There are three reasons for this.  First, the governments as well as the people reconcile themselves to the prevailing policy environment and prefer it to continue. Second, it is an accepted proposition that things that work should not be disturbed. Third, in all democratic societies, special interest groups adjust to the prevailing policy environment to maximise their share of societal income or wealth rather than adding to it. Mancur Olson calls them “distributional coalitions” (Rise and Decline of Nations, Yale University Press, 1982).  In other words, in all democratic societies, those who lose from the reforms are vengeful, while those who gain tend to be ungrateful. Thus, tax policy suffers from the tyranny of the status quo. In fact, even when reforms are undertaken due to some compulsion, they are seen as an event rather than a process that requires adjustments according to changing circumstances. How else can we explain the continued imperfections and distortions in tax systems despite their demonstrated shortcomings in design and implementation?  The “Fiscal Monitor” brought out by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in October has underlined the persisting distortions in the tax policies of emerging market economies (EMEs). To a considerable extent, this reflects the situation in India.  The international fiscal environment is fluid, with global debt expected to cross 100 per cent of gross domestic product by 2030, economies slowing down, prices rising, and interest rates remaining high and increasing further. Geopolitical hostilities, supply disruptions and the weaponisation of economic policies continue to keep energy prices high, growth subdued, the trade environment disturbed, and fiscal imbalances high due to stagnant revenues and elevated levels of defence spending.  In the prevailing subdued growth scenario, the concern is to improve productivity as much as the volume of investments. On the fiscal front, the focus will continue to be not merely to raise more revenues from taxes to contain the deficit but also to ensure that raising revenue does not create an additional burden through distortions. The issue, therefore, is not merely to reflect on how much to raise but also on the manner in which the revenue is raised.  In India, too, the battle to contain the fiscal deficit and debt levels must continue. The Sixteenth Finance Commission expects the general government debt to be limited to 73.1 per cent in 2030-31, from an estimated 77.1 per cent in 2026-27.  With the Union finance minister promising to reduce the Central government debt to 50 per cent, the states must compress it to 23.3 per cent in 2030-31, from almost 29.8 per cent estimated for the current year.  The continuing hostilities in West Asia are keeping energy prices elevated, while the drought situation in the country is adding to the woes. Elevated levels of consumer prices force the government to increase dearness allowance payments. Thus, the government is caught up in a situation where revenues are stagnant, current expenditures continue to escalate, and capital expenditures cannot be reduced without affecting the growth momentum, as private investment is yet to take off. With the country’s fiscal deficit exceeding the financial savings of the household sector, containing the deficit is imperative to avoid crowding out private investment and the government being pushed into a catch-22 situation.  The IMF’s Fiscal Monitor underlines four important sources of tax distortions adversely impacting economic activity in EMEs: (i)  the value added tax, which does not completely offset the taxes on business inputs, cascades through supply chains, raising costs and affecting competitiveness; (ii) tax differentials/incentives favouring certain assets, sectors, or firms over others driving investments away from most productive avenues.  Often, such incentives tend to exclude even rents from taxation; (iii) the personal income tax adversely affecting work effort when social safety nets are withdrawn as income increases; and (iv) complexities in administrative arrangements and compliance requirements in tax collection. Each one of the issues raised is relevant in the Indian context, and the government must take note of these and work towards remedying the problems if we are serious about increasing investment levels, productivity and competitiveness.  The economic costs of poor tax design and implementation can be considerable in emerging and developing economies. The report estimates that exemptions and non-registrations cause a 9 per cent loss in tax revenues, and eliminating such distortions can add to welfare gains of up to 0.8 per cent of gross domestic product. Tax incentives given to selected assets, sectors and firms increase the cost of capital by 15-20 per cent in these countries and, to that extent, discourage investment.  Rationalising the incentives and extending taxes on economic rents can increase the capital stock by 6.4 per cent in advanced countries and 8.2 per cent in low-income developing countries. The adverse effects on incentives and work effort get considerably weakened by poorly designed personal income taxes. Revenue-neutral reforms in the taxation of employment income can enhance employment rates by 1.2 percentage points, with the largest gains accruing to EMEs, particularly among lower-income earners. Similarly, reforms in tax administration can simplify the tax system, reduce administrative and compliance costs, narrow the productivity differential between large and small firms, and even help in designing better tax systems.  These recommendations have substantial relevance for reforming the Indian tax system. In the case of goods and services tax, the rationalisation exercise undertaken in September last year addresses the problems only partially. The tax system is still saddled with wide-ranging exemptions, with 148 commodities under the four-digit harmonised system of nomenclature (HSN) classification excluded.  In addition, the compounding system for taxpayers with less than ₹150 lakh turnover excludes a vast majority of resellers from availing input tax credit.  More importantly, the exclusion of petroleum products from GST has a severe cascading effect by escalating transportation costs.   The reforms initiated from November 1 this year to ease tax administration, compliance, and refunds are welcome, but the process has to continue. In the corporation income tax, there are still problems arising from discrimination between domestic and foreign companies. At a time when the country needs more foreign investment, the government would do well to ensure tax neutrality.  The Union finance minister has stated that the government is open to a relook at the capital gains tax regime. Indeed, there is no case in a modern economy for continuing with transaction taxes on securities or commodities. At the same time, the government would do well to eliminate many of the incentives in both personal and corporate income taxes to avoid unintended distortions, except in sectors considered clear winners. There are no grounds for optional tax exemptions and incentives under the personal income tax regime.    
           The writer, a councillor at Takshashila Institution, is former director, NIPFP.  The views are personal   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: India's workplace gender gap persists despite laws and high-profile firsts
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's workplace gender gap persists despite laws and high-profile firstsIndia's workplace gender gap persists despite laws and high-profile firsts

Women remain under-represented in Indian corporate leadership and earn less than men, highlighting the gap between workplace policies and actual gender equality.

premium

Gender diversity in corporate India remains a work in progress, with women under-represented in leadership roles and facing a significant pay gap, according to an ILO survey.

Kanika Datta5 min read Last Updated : Nov 11 2026 | 10:03 PM ISTEvery time a woman professional is appointed to a significant role for the first time, the media reports with breathless excitement. The first Indian woman to make partner in a Big Four firm, the first woman to head a bank, the first Indian woman to set up and receive approval for a mutual fund house, the first woman to head a financial watchdog or the competition regulator… all of these are duly hailed as unassailable signs of India’s march toward gender equality in the workplace. No interview of the woman concerned is complete without the obligatory question of “what it feels like to make it in a man’s world” or variations thereof. At the same time, few women in senior roles escape scrutiny on their appearance and attire.   No one has highlighted her irritation with this treatment more forcefully than Nirmala Sitharaman — yes, India’s first woman finance minister and currently the longest-serving one. A rarity in the Indian political firmament as a politician in her own right — not somebody’s wife, sister or mother — she has repeatedly stressed that she does not appreciate media discussions of her sari choices and appearance during the annual Budget presentation, pointing out that such observations put unnecessary stress on women.  Ms Sitharaman may be overstating the case; certainly, in this newspaper, her policies are subject to far more scrutiny than her appearance. But the larger point must be conceded. In the past three-plus decades, as women have begun to play a more conspicuous role in the white-collar executive world and public life in general, the routine practice of gender highlighting and the arch lines of questioning and commentary are revelatory. They actually tell you how little progress white-collar India has made in bridging the gender gap in the workplace.  This was clear from the latest International Labour Organization’s (ILO) survey, which shows that women remain hugely under-represented in Indian corporations and, worse, lag their male peers in earnings. This third edition of the survey, titled “Women in Business and Management: Scaling Success”, covered 11,957 enterprises in 99 countries. India accounted for the highest number of enterprises surveyed, with 768 respondents. Its findings are far from reassuring for a country that sees itself as an emerging global power.  Women accounted for just 12 per cent of managerial positions in India, putting it near the bottom (32nd) among 34 Asia-Pacific economies, ahead of only Pakistan and Bangladesh. Although women at the top are paid on a par with men, most women managers in India earn 28 per cent less than their male counterparts — the fourth-highest gender pay gap in Asia-Pacific. Only Tonga, the Republic of Korea (a surprise) and Vanuatu do worse.  The irony of this data is hard to miss. The past three decades have seen more federal laws and regulations enacted to enable corporations to provide a conducive environment for hiring women. From paid maternity benefits (upgraded in 2017) to paternity leave (1999), compulsory provision of crèches (2017), robust laws mandating protection against sexual harassment in the workplace (2013), and mandatory reservation of board seats for women (2014), India leads several advanced economies in this respect (the US, for instance, does not have a federal law guaranteeing paid maternity leave).  These policies have not resulted in a meaningful change in institutional gender balances because they are either not implemented, applied in such a perfunctory fashion as to make them useless in practice, or not tailored to socio-political realities. Maternity benefits and leave are a case in point. Most companies allow for the legal limit of 26 weeks of paid leave. Some more enlightened companies even allow up to 15 days of paternity leave (though there is no legal mandate for this in the private sector). The ILO survey shows that maternity benefits and support measures are rated the most effective initiatives to retain women. Yet, too many Indian organisations expect new mothers to resume the same level of efficiency and productivity as before. Though this is not an unreasonable expectation from the organisation’s point of view, it ignores the reality that the burden of childcare in India remains woman- and mother-centric, and explains why women leave in droves after they have children. In one of the ILO’s case studies, the Indian arm of the French media and advertising giant Havas introduced a successful “Maternity Bounce Back” initiative that helped new mothers manage their return, including part-time and hybrid work options.  Equally, traditional prejudices about “women’s jobs” constrain the ambit of employment. HR, accounting, and administration are considered posts fit for women to employ; marketing, maybe, but anything approaching consequential decision-making remains a male preserve, despite the presence of the mandatory woman appointee in the boardroom  It is increasingly clear that laws and regulations can only go so far in bridging the gender gap unless male-oriented managements shed their prejudices. Havas, which is headed by a man, has more than doubled the representation of women in its workforce from 19 to 43 per cent over four years by creating a targeted strategy to hire and retain women.  But its chief human resource officer underlined that the effort demands sustained hard work. Few corporations are willing to devote managerial mind-space to an issue seen as peripheral to the bottom line and disruptive of comfortable male-only cultures. So, women’s achievements will continue to be judged as gender-inflected exceptions rather than as part of a gender-neutral norm.   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Oil shock strains FY27 finances, but buffers may contain fiscal slippage
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Oil shock strains FY27 finances, but buffers may contain fiscal slippageOil shock strains FY27 finances, but buffers may contain fiscal slippage

Revenue and expenditure pressures are expected to widen the fiscal deficit, although the impact on market borrowings may be limited

premium

Aditi Nayar5 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 9:56 PM ISTOne of the casualties of the West Asia crisis has been the stress on oil-importing nations. Higher commodity prices, especially crude oil, have been transmitted, to varying degrees, into external account balances as well as inflation metrics, spurring rate hikes by several central banks, including India’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC). Another market concern stems from the widening fiscal deficit, potentially raising sovereign borrowing requirements.  While crude oil prices have yo-yoed through the year, the average price for the Indian basket of crude oil in the financial year so far (up to November 6, 2026) stands at about $102 per barrel. This would result in adverse outcomes via multiple channels, although the recent cooling in oil prices following the mid-terms in the United States, if sustained, may provide some much-awaited respite.  The oil & gas industry has been a key source of support for the exchequer, contributing as much as ₹4.8 trillion to the Government of India’s (GoI’s) finances, and another ₹3.4 trillion directly to the States’ exchequers in 2025-2026. Together, this amounted to a sizeable 2.4 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), equivalent to one-third of the estimated combined fiscal deficit of the GoI and the states. These cash flows are expected to come under stress in the ongoing financial year.  The GoI had already cut excise duty on petrol and diesel at the end of March 2026, giving oil marketing companies (OMCs) headroom to compensate for refining losses. With every ₹1/litre cut in such duties resulting in an estimated annual shortfall of ₹15,000 crore-16,000 crore, this measure would compress the GoI’s excise duty collections in FY27, although this would be partly offset by measures to shore up revenues from fuel exports.  Despite this, and the hikes in the retail selling prices of petrol and diesel through May 2026, the OMCs incurred substantial losses during Q1FY27. The sector’s contribution to the GoI in the form of corporation taxes and dividend income, which had amounted to about ₹59,600 crore and ₹25,700 crore, respectively, in FY26, is set to reduce in the ongoing fiscal.  Additionally, under recoveries of  OMCs on LPG, which stood at ₹62,000 crore by end-June 2026, are expected to exacerbate. The estimated loss per domestic cylinder was ₹500 in Q1 FY27 and remained at ₹300/cylinder in September 2026. Cumulative losses are likely to rise further if elevated international prices persist without a commensurate increase in domestic selling prices or additional government compensation, over and above the ₹30,000 crore approved in August 2025.    Further, the surge in prices of key raw materials, including LNG, and finished fertiliser prices, along with the depreciation of the USD/INR pair, render the GoI’s budgeted fertiliser subsidy amount of ₹1.71 trillion inadequate. Given the prevailing natural gas prices and international commodity prices, the subsidy requirement for the sector is expected to exceed the Budget Estimates by ₹0.8 trillion-1 trillion, and Icra expects the GoI to make additional allocations during the year.  Overall, these revenue and spending pressures are estimated to result in a material fiscal gap of  about ₹2.9 trillion in FY27, equivalent to 0.7 per cent of GDP.  However, a couple of shock absorbers could assuage a part of the pain. First, the Customs duty hikes on gold and silver to 15 per cent from 6 per cent earlier could net the GoI about ₹50,000 crore in the financial year.  Secondly, the GoI had allocated ~1 trillion towards the Economic Stabilisation Fund (ESF) as a part of its spending in FY26. Besides, the GoI’s stake sale in IDBI Bank is set to fetch it ~26,000 crore, which would take the miscellaneous capital receipts past the budgeted target of ~80,000 crore for FY27.  With this, we expect the fiscal slippage to be limited to 20 basis points above the budgeted target of 4.3 per cent of GDP for FY27. Additionally, the GoI could choose to pare discretionary expenditure, including capital spending, to further curtail the fiscal slippage, although this may dampen economic growth and be a sub-optimal solution. We estimate such savings, or the gap between approved and actual expenditure, to have amounted to ~1.6 trillion-1.7 trillion in FY26.  Regardless, fiscal slippage may not entirely manifest itself in higher market borrowings. Inflows under savings deposits, certificates and the Public Provident Fund have surged by 54 per cent in the first half of FY27, portending a considerable overshooting of the budgeted target on this front. This would provide some buffer to the GoI, even if bank deposit rates start to rise with the onset of the repo-rate hike cycle.  At present, we are pencilling in another rate hike from the MPC in December 2026, given the bleak outlook for food inflation. Subsequent hikes, if any, would take a cue from whether the crude-oil price eases further in the next few months, and its implications for the inflation outlook.    
 The writer is chief economist and head-research & outreach at Icra     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : Fiscal Deficit BS Opinion West Asia oil crisis

entry.title: Post-1991 reforms left India short on manufacturing, growth and jobs
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Post-1991 reforms left India short on manufacturing, growth and jobsPost-1991 reforms left India short on manufacturing, growth and jobs

Three decades after 1991, it is clear India needs a new policy approach

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Nitin Desai6 min read Last Updated : Nov 10 2026 | 9:50 PM ISTThe year 1991 is seen as a key point of transition in the Indian economy, from its earlier preference for the public sector to the promotion of the private sector. A popular explanation for this change is the removal of the industrial licensing Act in 1991. There is a widespread belief that this delicensing accelerated economic growth. How correct is this belief?  The shift from the public to the private sector has certainly taken place, not just in manufacturing but also in infrastructure. The share of the public sector in manufacturing investment had started declining from 1980-81, when it was around 40 per cent, to 24 per cent in 1991-92, owing to some early liberalisation moves. The decline in the public sector’s share in manufacturing investment continued thereafter, falling further to 8 per cent in 2023-24. This is one measure of the shift from the public sector to the private sector.  The other shift came in infrastructure development, with the private sector being promoted as the supplier of electricity, the constructor of roads, and the manager of airports and seaports. Because of this, there was a decline in the share of public-sector investment in infrastructure from around 69 per cent in 1991-92 to 44 per cent in 2023-24.  Did this shift from the public to the private sector accelerate manufacturing growth? The answer regrettably is that it did not do so. The share of manufacturing in gross value added (GVA), at current prices, rose from about 12 per cent in 1950-51 to 18-19 per cent by the mid-1990s, fluctuated a little and stayed at that level till 2010-11. It has since declined steadily to reach 14 per cent by 2024-25. The share of manufacturing in total investment has also fallen from 41 per cent in 2011-12 to 32 per cent in 2023-24. The percentage share of manufacturing in employment remains at 10-11 per cent. Only three Indian companies figure in the list of the top 100 non-US companies by market capitalisation. Frankly, the delicensing done in 1991 has not accelerated the contribution of manufacturing to growth.  Delicensing has had some impact on the advance of newcomers. It has also facilitated a major expansion of conglomerates — Tata, Reliance, Aditya Birla and Adani have expanded rapidly, with their market cap going up massively. The notable ones being a 1000-fold increase in the market capitalisation of Reliance and the emergence of Adani.  They have diversified their investment into a variety of mostly low-medium technology areas, including retailing. They do not have a substantial presence in the global economy. Some part of their expansion, particularly in infrastructure, is a product not of delicensing but of active support from the government. Government support for specific companies has not been eroded by delicensing.  If we look at emerging countries that have done well with exports and technology development, we find large firms that are specialised in a few areas rather than conglomerates with widely diverse activities. China is a remarkable example. In the early 1990s, the difference between India and China in terms of their share of manufacturing was marginal. Today, China’s manufacturing output is nearly 10 times that of India’s and includes a significant share of high-technology products. China has 17 companies in the list of top 100 non-US market companies, and many of them were new starters. The big difference between China and India lies in our much weaker performance in new technologically-led startups.  Compared to delicensing, the opening up of the financial system to the private sector has had a greater impact on private sector development. Private-sector banks have increased their share of total bank advances from 17 per cent in 2004-05 to 39 per cent in 2024-25. Their share of total bank employees has also risen substantially, from 10 per cent to 43 per cent over the same period.  The other big change was the liberalisation of private mutual funds, which now have shot up to a level where they are managing ~87 trillion of assets. These two developments, along with a substantial simplification of trading in shares, have led to a transformed financial system, with market capitalisation rising close to 120 per cent of nominal GDP.  The most substantive post-1991 change has been the extraordinary boom in the export of software services. India’s software exports have grown from just $400 million in 1991-92 (less than 2 per cent of total exports) to $240 billion in 2025-26 — a 600-fold increase. They now account for 28 per cent of exports and employ around 6 million people. However, the software boom that fuelled export and employment growth now faces a major global challenge from artificial intelligence.  The foundation for this software services boom was laid in a 1981 landmark report by a committee headed by V Rajaraman that proposed concessions for the import of computers in order to facilitate software exports. This proposal was accepted in 1983, reversing an earlier policy that focused on protecting mainly public-sector companies producing electronic goods. This import liberalisation also facilitated computerisation in banking, air and rail reservations. But the big economic impact came with the rise in software exports, particularly after the special role that Indian enterprises had in making the software changes required to cope with the millennial change at the end of the century.  There were several reports on liberalisation in the pre-1990 era, and some were partially implemented. One far reaching one was the report submitted in 1979 by the Committee on Controls and Subsidies chaired by Vadilal Dagli and commissioned by Morarji Desai. The report criticised the industrial licensing system, arguing that it had ceased to serve the goals of national planning. It recommended a shift from physical output quotas to fiscal and financial instruments, called for the dissolution of the Controller of Capital Issues (CCI), and criticised subsidies on food and fertilisers. However, the report was shelved after a new government came to power following the 1980 elections, and several of its recommendations were implemented only after 1991.  The drive for liberalisation and strengthening growth prospects goes back to the 1980s, while the substantive implementation came after 1991. However, average GDP growth since 1991 has not been significantly higher than in the 1980s. We must also recognise that we have fallen short in two crucial sectors — agriculture and manufacturing — and need to rethink our policy approach to both. We must also recognise that post-1991 policies supporting the private sector have not done enough to improve the lives of lower-income groups and generate employment. Hence, we need to rethink policies today because the reforms of the 1990s are no longer sufficient.

entry.title: Chatroom: Clearing doubts on SEZ drawback claims and EOU job work
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Chatroom: Clearing doubts on SEZ drawback claims and EOU job workChatroom: Clearing doubts on SEZ drawback claims and EOU job work

Experts clarify SEZ drawback procedures, the scope of newly amended rules and compliance requirements for EOUs sending imported raw materials for job work

premium

A cargo ship carrying containers at an Indian port (Representative Image) (Photo: Shutterstock)

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Nov 09 2026 | 10:52 PM ISTWe refer to the Commerce Ministry notification dated October 30, 2026, amending Rule 24(2) of the SEZ Rules, 2006. It refers to drawback or “any other similar scheme” laid down under the Customs and Central Excise Duties Drawback Rules, 2017, as amended from time to time. Which similar schemes have been notified under those Rules?   The expression “any other similar scheme” is unclear because the amendment does not identify any such scheme. I am not aware of any separate similar scheme notified under those rules. Mere similarity to drawback is insufficient: the scheme must also be laid down under the specified drawback rules. The intention may be to accommodate introduction of a similar scheme under those rules in future. The words “as amended from time to time” indicate that possibility, but this remains an inference rather than an expressly stated purpose.  The amended rule requires the SEZ Unit, Developer or Domestic Tariff Area supplier to claim drawback from the Specified Officer, retaining the disclaimer requirement where the supplier claims. Does this displace the procedure under CBIC Circular Nos. 43/2007-Cus. dated December 5, 2007, 39/2010-Cus. dated October 15, 2010, and 24/2017-Cus. dated June 30, 2017, directing DTA suppliers to their jurisdictional Customs authorities?  In my view, the amended rule prescribes the SEZ Specified Officer as the authority before whom the DTA supplier must claim drawback. It does not expressly provide two alternative routes. Earlier administrative circulars cannot prevail to the extent that they conflict with the amended statutory rule. However, leaving those instructions unreconciled creates practical uncertainty. CBIC should promptly clarify the revised filing and disbursement procedure, brand-rate fixation, treatment of earlier supplies and pending claims.  We are an EOU. Can we send our duty-free imported raw materials directly from the port to a job worker and receive the processed goods for further processing and export?  No. The imported raw materials must first reach the EOU and be accounted for before being sent for job work. Paragraph 3 of CBEC Circular No. 67/98-Cus. dated September 14, 1998, requires prior receipt and accounting of imported or indigenous raw materials at the unit. Paragraph 6 of Circular No. 54/2004-Cus. dated October 13, 2004, expressly prohibits sending goods directly to the job worker without bringing them into the unit. Condition 3(a) of Notification No. 52/2003-Cus. dated March 31, 2003, requires bringing the goods into the unit and using them for the specified purpose. Condition 3(b) requires proper accounting for their receipt, storage and utilisation. Although Rule 7 of the Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty or for Specified End Use) Rules, 2022 permits job work, it does not override the exemption conditions. Rule 3(1)(g) requires job work to be consistent with the notification. Rule 11(2) preserves the importer’s responsibility to ensure that goods are used for the purposes provided in that notification. These provisions support compliance with the exemption conditions; they do not independently dispense with the requirement of prior receipt at the EOU.

entry.title: India's video audience is shifting as streaming rewrites viewing habits
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / India's video audience is shifting as streaming rewrites viewing habitsIndia's video audience is shifting as streaming rewrites viewing habits

From 10-second episodes to 10-hour seasons, the deluge brought by streaming and on-demand services is now changing how Indians entertain themselves

premium

A viewer watches streaming content on a smartphone as OTT platforms reshape India’s entertainment landscape

Vanita Kohli-Khandekar5 min read Last Updated : Nov 09 2026 | 10:10 PM ISTSheldon Cooper, Leonard Hofstadter, Rajesh Koothrappali, and Howard Wolowitz work at the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech. The journey of these socially inept scientists as they bumble through life, relationships, and work conundrums makes for a witty, wise, and hugely popular show.  The Big Bang Theory (CBS) began in 2007 and ended with 12 seasons in 2019. It is a global hit that has been licensed across streaming platforms. This columnist has watched and rewatched it dozens of times on Netflix. Ditto for its spinoff, Young Sheldon (2017-2024; seven seasons). Not surprisingly, then, the algorithm kept pushing reels from the latest spinoff, Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage, until I found it on JioHotstar. The titles may vary, but the journey for each of us is similar — you see some reels, or someone you know does, and you end up watching a show or a film on OTT.  Ten years ago, in 2016, you probably watched Nagin, The Kapil Sharma Show or Bigg Boss on TV. Netflix and Amazon Prime Video had just come into India. YouTube had been around for eight years but was used, largely, for search, to listen to music or to figure things out. If you were young, you might have watched series like TVF’s Little Things or Tripling that began on YouTube. Streaming has changed what we watch and how we watch it, but a decade ago, it wasn’t quite the force it is now.  Three fabulously done recent reports capture different parts of this change.  The first, IMDB’s “Ten Years of Streaming in India” uses the 250 million monthly visitors to IMDB worldwide to list the top 10 shows (Mirzapur, Criminal Justice, The Family Man, The B***s of Bollywood, Sacred Games etc), the biggest creators (TVF, Applause, D2R Films), the stars (Pankaj Tripathi, Manoj Bajpayee), the streamers (Netflix, JioHotstar, Prime Video, YouTube, among others). The shift from overwhelmingly crime-led programming to broader genres reflects the evolution of the audience and of the creative ecosystem.  The report doesn’t say this, but what is evident is that, as streamers attempt to scale, they are doing what TV did — get as much of India on their service as possible. That explains why Netflix brought The Kapil Sharma Show or India’s got Latent to its service or why Prime Video aggregates dozens of other services from BBC’s iPlayer to SonyLIV.  Much of this comes on the back of some stellar storytelling. Three of the six most durable franchises mentioned in the report — Mirzapur, The Family Man (Prime Video) and Criminal Justice (JioHotstar) — have built worlds that audiences love to revisit to see the characters they have grown fond of: Kaleen Bhaiya, Madhav Mishra, and Srikant Tiwari. Then, there is Panchayat, a sweet, slow look at village life and politics that continues to charm audiences over four seasons, with a fifth in the offing. Musafir Café, Pritam and Pedro are the other gentler shows that move away from the “edgy” obsession that characterised the first round of growth. This abundance of shows and stories has generated revenue, but largely at the expense of television rather than by creating a significantly larger market.  That brings this to the second piece of recent research. The Media Partners Asia (MPA) latest numbers show that India’s “screen economy” has gone from $9.5 billion in 2021 to $12.4 billion by the end of this year. Streaming brings in half of this at $6 billion — linear TV is down from over $7 billion to just under $5 billion this year. As the MPA presentation puts it, India has the largest audience, but the smallest wallet.  “India generates under $10 per head from screens versus $890 in the US. That gap is the runway.” It estimates that India will hit $15.4 billion across screens by 2031, a compounded annual growth rate of 5 per cent against 2 for China, Japan and Korea.  The MPA data has another tiny number of $0.3 billion for microdramas. This brings us to the third report. “Microdramas — The India Story”, an audience research report by Ormax Media and Meta, shows that, unlike big-screen streaming, which is somewhat male-skewed (57:43), microdramas, which are watched mostly on the mobile phone, have a female skew (55:45).  This mirrors China and the US, the two largest microdrama markets, where women over 50 make up half the audience. In China, two-thirds of this audience is from Tier-III towns and rural areas. The same is true of India, where viewership is skewed towards urban and rural markets with populations of less than one million. The only similarity with streaming is that a bulk — three-fourths — of the money comes from advertising. Audiences simply don’t pay. In fact, most consumers in India have no clue where they watched a microdrama or what the story was — it is simply “social media” to them.  From 10-second episodes to 10-hour seasons, the deluge brought by streaming and on-demand services is now rapidly rewiring audiences. Add artificial intelligence to the mix, and there is no telling what the next set of reports will reveal.

entry.title: Fit-and-proper decisions: Regulators need clear, predictable rules
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Fit-and-proper decisions: Regulators need clear, predictable rulesFit-and-proper decisions: Regulators need clear, predictable rules

Regulators need discretion, but that discretion must be structured, transparent and predictable

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

M S SahooSumit Agrawal6 min read Last Updated : Nov 09 2026 | 9:56 PM ISTIn the quarter ended June 2026, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) cancelled the registrations of 207 insolvency professionals (IPs) “on failing to fulfil the requirement of fit and proper person status”, roughly 5 per cent of registered IPs. No order explaining these cancellations is publicly available. The profession, and the creditors and courts who rely on it, cannot know what made these IPs unfit, or what might make the next one so.  In the same quarter, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) moved in the opposite direction. It amended its regulations to mandate that a person be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before being declared not a “fit and proper person”. It also removed two triggers that, since November 2021, had automatically rendered a person unfit: A pending criminal complaint or FIR filed by Sebi, and a pending chargesheet filed by any enforcement agency in a matter concerning economic offences. Sebi noted that there is no judicial application of mind at the FIR or complaint stage, and, even at the chargesheet stage, the allegation has not been adjudicated. The change followed public consultation and despite some comments favouring retention of the provisions. Sebi also approved administrative steps to withdraw pending show-cause notices that would not survive the amended test. This is a welcome instance of regulation correcting itself through consultation.  That correction settles one question: An allegation should not operate as a verdict. It does not, however, eliminate wide regulatory discretion. Some elements of the fit and proper test are objective and readily verifiable: Whether a person has been convicted of specified offences, debarred by a regulatory authority, or classified as a fugitive economic offender. Others are inherently subjective, requiring an assessment of integrity, honesty, ethical conduct, reputation, fairness and character. More significantly, these criteria are expressly illustrative, not exhaustive. The regulations permit Sebi to consider “any criteria as it deems fit” and to specify “any other disqualification” from time to time. This gives the regulator considerable latitude to assess unspecified considerations against open-ended standards.  Such discretion may be justified by the need to protect market integrity and investors, but it also increases regulatory uncertainty, reduces the predictability of market entry and creates scope for inconsistent decision-making. Importantly, the regulatory framework enables Sebi not merely to apply prescribed eligibility norms but, in effect, to supplement and shape them. The boundary between its quasi-legislative function of prescribing eligibility standards and its executive function of applying those standards consequently becomes blurred. This raises questions of transparency, accountability and institutional design, particularly where executive discretion can effectively determine the content of the eligibility standards themselves.  The omitted triggers have not left the room. Sebi has said that pending criminal proceedings of a severe nature remain relevant under the principle-based criteria, to be weighed case by case. That is defensible in principle. But “severe” is undefined. So is “economic offence”, which Sebi did not define on the grounds that the category keeps evolving. Sebi has left open the possibility of guidelines on when pending proceedings may be egregious enough to disqualify a person. In the public consultation, concerns were expressed that the omitted clauses should not simply migrate into guidelines. The concern is legitimate: A regulator can reach through the principles door the very outcome that the rules door had produced.  The choice between rules and principles is old. Rules are relatively cheap to administer and predictable, but can be over-inclusive: They place the cost of a crude boundary on whoever lands on its wrong side, as the 2021 triggers did. Principles fit the facts better, but are costlier to apply and create scope for inconsistency and selective enforcement. The answer is not to swing from one to the other, but to discipline judgement so that it delivers the predictability that rules provide. Five elements could help.  First, publish the factors in advance. Where pending proceedings are relevant, the regulator should specify, after consultation, what it will weigh: The nature and gravity of the allegation, its nexus to the regulated activity, the stage reached (FIR, chargesheet, framing of charges, conviction under appeal), the passage of time, and the person’s conduct since.  Second, reason and publish every order. A declaration of unfitness should be a speaking order, published with suitable redaction, so that individual decisions accumulate into a body of precedent. The 207 cancellations would then instruct the profession rather than unsettle it.  Third, calibrate the consequences. Between fit and unfit lie conditions, enhanced disclosure, monitoring and exclusion from particular functions. A binary test can push a regulator towards either overreach or inaction.  Fourth, build in reversibility. A finding resting on pending proceedings should carry a review date and be revisited on discharge, quashing or acquittal, with rights restored on final exoneration. Sebi has declined automatic restoration on a stay; restoration on an outcome should at least be expressly provided for.  Fifth, create new disqualifications only through regulations. The residual power to specify “any other disqualification” should be exercised through regulations backed by consultation and a regulatory impact assessment, not through subsidiary instructions.  These are not Sebi's questions alone. The IBBI’s regulations likewise allow it to take into account any consideration it deems fit. The Reserve Bank of India, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, and the International Financial Services Centres Authority all run versions of the same test. A common minimum standard of structured discretion, rather than a separate experiment by each regulator, would serve markets and professionals alike.  Sebi has shown that a regulator can recognise that a rule has gone too far and correct it through consultation. The harder task is to demonstrate that judgement, once freed from a rigid checklist, can be exercised in the open. A fit and proper test earns trust only when those subject to it can understand, from published criteria and reasons, what makes a person fit, and what does not.  
 The writers are, respectively, former chairperson of IBBI; and  managing partner, Regstreet Law Advisors, and a former Sebi officer     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Empty bank accounts in Vigilance Week expose gaps in banking oversight
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Empty bank accounts in Vigilance Week expose gaps in banking oversightEmpty bank accounts in Vigilance Week expose gaps in banking oversight

Are IT-trained staff available when regular operators are on leave? Are daily-waged support workers restricted to non-sensitive areas? Banks need to address these questions

premium

Representative image for bank

Tamal Bandyopadhyay8 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 8:11 PM ISTFarmer Vijendra Singh lost money kept with a bank. Singh told the media that his savings account at a branch of Punjab National Bank (PNB) in Greater Noida once held approximately ₹87–88 lakh, including compensation received from the authorities for land acquisition. When he checked, the balance had fallen to barely ₹1 lakh.  He is one of many depositors whose money, they allege, had disappeared from savings accounts and fixed deposits without their authorisation.  This happened in the last week of October when the banking industry was observing Vigilance Awareness Week.  Since 2000, every year, during the week that includes the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (October 31), a nationwide campaign has been organised by the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) to promote integrity, transparency, and the fight against corruption in public governance. This year, it was observed from October 26 to November 1 on the theme ‘Probity for Prosperity’.  Government departments, central public sector enterprises, public sector banks, and other participating organisations were directed to begin the observance with an integrity pledge. Workshops, outreach programmes, debates, quizzes,  and other awareness activities were also encouraged.  The vigilance-related activities are not confined to just one week. The CVC’s three-month preventive-vigilance campaign this year, running from August 17 to November 16, identifies five priorities: Disposal of pending complaints, disposal of pending cases, capacity building, digital initiatives, and transparency in contract management and awarding contracts to vendors. Work under these priority heads will continue till November 30.  The initiative is great. But, beyond meetings and posters, awareness must reach branch counters. All banks must remain vigilant 24/7 through an ever-aware oversight machinery. Not pledges and activities — the real scorecard is the number of vulnerable pockets closed within the system.  The Greater Noida allegations concern savings and fixed-deposit accounts, including those of farmers who had deposited land-compensation money. Customers say transactions occurred without their consent and allege that they received no SMS alerts. The bank concerned, I understand, has assured all aggrieved depositors of refunds within a few days. Media reports also hint at unauthorised access to lockers and growing anxiety among NRI customers. I have not been able to independently corroborate such allegations.  Scenes of distressed depositors waiting for explanations may evoke memories of troubled cooperative banks. But this bank is not insolvent, and only a tiny fraction of deposits is affected. Therefore, customers need not panic.  However, the institution’s immediate task is twofold: Establish the facts and prevent uncertainty from becoming a second injury. The bank’s preliminary inquiry identified approximately ₹ 10.24 crore in suspected unauthorised withdrawals, even as reconciliation continues to establish the full extent of the fraud. Earlier, customer allegations put the amount at nearly ₹ 35 crore, a figure that has not been officially confirmed.  A November 1 media report noted that a first information report (FIR) filed with the police mentions transactions worth ₹12.12 crore, while a branch staff member speaking anonymously told a social media channel that approximately 35 account holders had approached the police, with alleged unauthorised transactions pegged at around ₹17 crore.  These are overlapping investigative and complaint-based figures. By November 3, the Central Bureau of Investigation had reportedly arrested two individuals—a bank office assistant and an outsider—in connection with the alleged ₹ 10.24-crore fraud case. Arrest or suspension does not establish guilt, and the investigation into other possible accomplices and the movement of funds continues.  PNB’s October 30 statement said it had settled three claims totalling ₹43 lakh and would honour all genuine and valid claims. Going by the FIR, one woman depositor found three unfamiliar transactions dated September 16, 2026, when she updated her passbook. She had neither authorised nor consented to them.  The subsequent inquiry reportedly found that credentials belonging to six bank officials had been used for unauthorised transactions. Whether those credentials were shared voluntarily or compromised remains part of the investigation.  Other reported allegations include the manipulation of customer details and fixed-deposit records, premature closures, and diversion of funds through beneficiary accounts. The suspected activities had reportedly been going on for about three years. Why did the institution need a customer’s complaint to identify a pattern that its own internal controls should have flagged? The investigation must establish whether system alerts were absent, inadequately designed, ignored, or improperly closed. It must also determine which officials had access to the relevant information and what action they took.  National figures underline the gravity of the issue. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) Annual Report for 2025–26 records 10,114 fraud cases involving ₹48,021 crore, compared with 23,722 cases involving ₹32,803 crore in the preceding year. The data covers frauds of ₹1 lakh and above, and cases reported in a given year may relate to events from earlier years. Also, the FY2025-26 figure includes ₹30,199 crore relating to 314 older cases reported afresh following a re-examination. Crucially, the amount involved in reported frauds does not necessarily represent the final loss.  Reports of surprise inspections at PNB spoke of outsiders working inside banking areas, including cash counters and on branch computers. Initial reporting put the number of suspended branch heads at around 20. A recent media report revised the figure to around 50. Claims that suspensions may have reached nearly 100 remain unverified.  The bank’s inspection at the branches involved found that individuals — including insurance-company personnel, recovery agents, and other helpers — were allegedly assisting with core banking work amid claims of staffing shortages. Business correspondents, insurance representatives, and temporary workers may have legitimate, defined duties. But their presence does not justify access to another employee’s password, unrestricted customer information, or transaction-authorisation powers. Staffing shortages cannot be an excuse for password sharing, and management cannot treat staffing levels as unrelated to financial controls.  Can a branch maintain a genuine dual-control separation between the person entering a transaction and the person approving it? Are sufficiently IT-trained staff available when the regular operator of a specific desk goes on leave? Are support workers hired on a daily-wage basis properly engaged, supervised, and strictly restricted to non-sensitive areas? What happens when a manager formally reports that safe working arrangements cannot be maintained?  The reported reliance on informal helpers should prompt a serious re-examination of recruitment and deployment policies, including support-staff arrangements — rather than an assumption that daily-wage labour is an acceptable substitute for controlled system access.  Management must also examine whether third-party sales targets and other performance pressures leave sufficient time for the daily verification of transactions, reconciliation of all non-customer accounts, and prompt complaint handling.  Finally, auditors should examine repeated debits and credits, ledger reversals, connected beneficiaries, and changes to deposit instructions. They must scrutinise premature fixed deposit closures, changes to maturity-proceeds credit accounts, modifications to account operating details, registered mobile number alterations, disabled alert preferences, and unusual staff access patterns.  Following the RBI’s Master Direction on Fraud Risk Management (issued on July 31, 2026), banks require board-approved arrangements covering prevention, detection, investigation, staff accountability, recovery, and reporting. A dedicated board committee carries the responsibility for reviewing frauds, root causes, and corrective measures. The directions also call for early warning mechanisms covering non-credit banking transactions, with monitoring designed to promptly identify unusual activity. PNB’s experience with the 2018 Nirav Modi scandal makes the need for durable institutional learning particularly vital. Following that event, the RBI discontinued Letters of Undertaking (LoUs) for import trade credit.  For a depositor awaiting access to savings, a mere institutional explanation is not a resolution. The bank should provide a dedicated claims officer, written acknowledgements, clear verification requirements, and regular progress updates. Restoration of funds must transparently cover applicable interest alongside the principal amount, without unjust charges. For Singh and other complainants, the test is not whether employees raised their hands to take a pledge during Vigilance Awareness Week. It is whether the institution can explain what happened, restore legitimate claims, and demonstrate that the next depositor will not face the same ordeal.  Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel’s standard for public service remains a fitting measure of that responsibility. In 1947, while addressing civil service probationers, Patel said: “No service worth the name can claim to exist if it does not have in view the achievement of the highest standard of integrity.”

entry.title: What to prioritise: Debt repayment, insurance, or investing your money?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / What to prioritise: Debt repayment, insurance, or investing your money?What to prioritise: Debt repayment, insurance, or investing your money?

An investment plan should begin with financial protection and debt repayment, not market returns

premium

Financial planning for young professionals should begin with adequate insurance and debt repayment before moving to investments, says Harsh Roongta. | Representative Picture

Harsh Roongta4 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 8:09 PM ISTI was talking to Rohini, who had just got her commercial pilot licence and begun her first job with an airline. She wanted my advice on investing the monthly surplus from her salary. She had an education loan at 8 per cent interest, with eight years to run. Her surplus was what remained after the hefty equated monthly instalment (EMI). I told her there was an order to follow. First, pay the fixed EMI on the loan. Second, buy the right insurance. Third, use the balance to repay the loan faster. Investing comes after that.She was shocked. “I thought an investment adviser would tell me where to invest. Instead, you ask me to buy insurance, though you write against it in your columns. And you want me to repay my loan faster.”  After her shock wore off, I explained my position. I have always written against the mis-selling of insurance. Yet the right insurance comes before any investment. Rohini said she had no dependants, so she did not need term insurance. But she herself depended on her income. That income needed protection. She needed two covers: a critical illness policy that pays a lump sum on diagnosis of a listed illness and an accidental disability policy that pays if an accident disables her permanently. That money would replace her lost income.The airline already gave sufficient cover for both risks. It also covered her medical costs. I told her to buy her own medical policy. It is unwise to depend solely on an employer’s policy.  That brought us to step three: repaying the loan faster. Rohini had two fears. The first was liquidity. Investments could be redeemed in an emergency, but could she access money used to prepay the loan? Her lender allowed her to withdraw any amount she had prepaid. She could also build an emergency fund from the surplus before beginning loan prepayment. The fear of missing out (FOMO) came second. Her friends were making returns from all kinds of ideas. She would be stuck with the boring task of repaying a loan.  My response was simple. I asked her if she would borrow at 8 per cent to invest in any idea, however good. She was horrified at the thought. I told her investing her surplus instead of repaying the loan was the same thing. It is borrowing to invest. Repaying the loan early saves her interest at a rate of 8 per cent. Equity could earn more over 8-10 years, but that return is uncertain. Returns can come in bursts after long spells of losses. She may lose patience and quit at the wrong time. A systematic investment plan (SIP) can be stopped. An EMI cannot. In uncertain times, it is best to have as little committed repayment as possible.  Rohini said her father might clear the loan. Where would she then invest her surplus? Her friends were investing in cryptocurrencies, unlisted shares, unregulated start-ups and initial public offerings (IPOs). I told her to avoid such get-rich-quick ideas. She should save 30 per cent of her salary every month. Her living costs and insurance premiums must fit within the rest. She should not wait for the perfect investment. At this stage of her career, the compounding of her savings habit matters more than the compounding of her investments. I suggested a simple passive fund: an index, multi-asset or hybrid fund. If choosing was hard, even a bank recurring deposit would do.  Truth be told, Rohini expected an investment adviser to tell her where to invest. But an adviser must look at her financial life, beginning with whether she should invest at all. My advice was boring and gave her no bragging rights. She understood the reasoning and followed it. She bought the right insurance. She cleared the loan from her own income, though her father could have helped, and then started a monthly SIP in a passive multi-asset fund. Good advice is like a kandeel on a dark path. It does not dazzle. It lights the next few steps. I wish every reader the same light and the courage to follow it.
